title: The Milky Way Bar, Spiral Arms and Galactic Disc Dynamics as Tests of the Frame

lessons.title: Lesson 1 — Settle in.
paragraphs: Welcome in. I am Professor Milos Wisniewski, and this is The Milky Way Bar, Spiral Arms and Galactic Disc Dynamics as Tests of the Frame. This is lesson 1 of 1 in the full thirty-minute build of this class. In this lesson we take the class's own material in order — nothing here is imported, and nothing is asked later that is not taught here first. We begin here: Settle in.

Settle in. I am Professor Milos Wisniewski, and this is The Milky Way Bar, Spiral Arms and Galactic Disc Dynamics as Tests of the Frame. This class is built on real papers — deposited, citable work. I will present each paper and what it reports; that presentation is the lesson. At the end I will ask you questions on what was taught here — nothing else.
Here is the next piece of the material, in the order the class presents it.

'A Bar Pattern Speed for the Milky Way Inferred from Resonance Locations in a Flat Rotation Curve'. Its stated result: Headline result (values verbatim from results.json): pattern_speed_kms_per_kpc = 36.67; inner_lindblad_radius_kpc = 1.757; outer_lindblad_radius_kpc = 10.24. These values were computed by the deposited compute.py from published survey values, under the assumptions stated in the paper.
Now we go one step further into the material.

'A Consistency Check of the Oort Constants Against the Galactic Rotation Curve'. Its stated result: Headline result (values verbatim from results.json): circular_speed_implied_kms = 220.9; epicyclic_frequency_kms_per_kpc = 35.98; kappa_to_Omega_ratio = 1.323. These values were computed by the deposited compute.py from published survey values, under the assumptions stated in the paper.
The next piece is where this starts to come together.

'A Mass Decomposition Bound for the Milky Way Rotation Curve at the Solar Circle'. Its stated result: Headline result (values verbatim from results.json): halo_contribution_kms = 126.1; enclosed_mass_1e10_msun = 9.14; mass_fraction_halo_within_R0 = 0.3285. These values were computed by the deposited compute.py from published survey values, under the assumptions stated in the paper.
Listen carefully here — this piece carries weight in the questions later.

'A Test of Disc Self-Gravity from the Local Scale Height and Surface Density'. Its stated result: Headline result (values verbatim from results.json): predicted_scale_height_pc = 211.5; predicted_to_observed_ratio = 0.705; implied_surface_density_msun_per_pc2 = 49.34. These values were computed by the deposited compute.py from published survey values, under the assumptions stated in the paper.
We take the pieces in order, because each one stands on the last.

'Bounding the Corotation Radius of the Milky Way Bar from the Bar Length and the Fast-Bar Condition'. Its stated result: Headline result (values verbatim from results.json): corotation_central_kpc = 6; corotation_min_kpc = 4.5; corotation_max_kpc = 7.7. These values were computed by the deposited compute.py from published survey values, under the assumptions stated in the paper.
Stay with me, because the next piece builds directly on that one.

'Bounding the Local Dark Matter Density from Vertical Kinematics of Disc Stars'. Its stated result: Headline result (values verbatim from results.json): surface_density_excess_msun_per_pc2 = 23; local_dark_matter_density_msun_per_pc3 = 0.0115; local_dark_matter_density_GeV_per_cm3 = 0.437. These values were computed by the deposited compute.py from published survey values, under the assumptions stated in the paper.
Here is the next piece of the material, in the order the class presents it.

Now my worked example — this class's set problem, worked in full. The problem: Take the paper “A Bar Pattern Speed for the Milky Way Inferred from Resonance Locations in a Flat Rotation Curve”. Its stated result is: Headline result (values verbatim from results.json): pattern_speed_kms_per_kpc = 36.67; inner_lindblad_radius_kpc = 1.757; outer_lindblad_radius_kpc = 10.24. These values were computed by the deposited compute.py from published survey values, under the assumptions stated in the paper. (a) Restate the claim in your own words. (b) Name one observation or computation that could prove it wrong. The worked answer: A strong answer restates the claim without borrowing the paper’s wording, then names a test the paper itself would accept — here, the natural test is to recompute or re-measure the headline quantity in the stated result and check it against the paper’s own number, under the paper’s own stated assumptions.

Let us gather what this lesson taught, in order: Settle in; 'A Bar Pattern Speed for the Milky Way Inferred from Resonance Locations in a Flat Rotation Curve'; 'A Consistency Check of the Oort Constants Against the Galactic Rotation Curve'; 'A Mass Decomposition Bound for the Milky Way Rotation Curve at the Solar Circle'; 'A Test of Disc Self-Gravity from the Local Scale Height and Surface Density'; 'Bounding the Corotation Radius of the Milky Way Bar from the Bar Length and the Fast-Bar Condition'. Those are the pieces — hold them in that order, because the questions follow the same road.

That is the lesson, whole. Below it are the questions — every one of them drawn from what was just taught, and nothing else. The full text of this lesson stays open beside the questions, and going back to read a piece again is learning, not cheating. When you are ready, begin.
